Belgian incorporation/religious policy349 and separate revolt/urban-integration350 paths retain rural resistance versus pragmatic bourgeois accommodation. Economic benefit is not worded as adoption of French nationality.
Venice partition and Bonaparte Venetian partition360–361 retrieve resistance/Verona as pretext and Austrian territorial gains; no liberation claim substitutes for the bargain.
Italian unification movement is a direct conceptual route across all six treatments, distinguishing patriot aspiration, French obstruction, symbols, regional consolidation and radical frustration.

Batavian fiscal exploitation346–347, economic crisis347 and invasion/dependence346–347 expose different British blockade and French extraction costs plus the lack of a viable alternative. Relative internal autonomy remains a qualified explanation in the reached passage, not independence.

Sanfedist movement and Ruffo364–365 reach organization, social/religious mobilization, feudal concessions, disorder and restraint. The wording does not equate autonomous local vendettas with the later court’s deliberate reprisals.

Rhineland incorporation351–352 and Cis-Rhenan proposal351 retrieve competing French calculations, Hoche’s alternative, practical departmentalization and weak local consent. They do not promise a popular national mandate or silently merge practical and final legal annexation.

Dutch economic burdens346–347 and invasion346–347 retrieve trade, industry, poor relief and military dependency alongside the test of Orangist loyalty; neutrality and restoration are not equated.

Belgian annexation348, religious policy349, Peasants War349–350 and differing responses350 explicitly connect extraction, recruitment and parish religion while distinguishing rural insurgency from urban reactions.

Lombard extraction/Pavia358–359, Cisalpine361–363, Roman362–363 and resistance366–367 provide the requested comparison of religion, fiscal burdens and town-country conflict. Distinct local mechanisms remain visible.

Coalition collapse and Bonaparte departure368 connect reverses, exhausted resources and local hostility with his decision to leave Egypt; return374 supplies the political opportunity without asserting an exclusively public motive.

Italian Jacobins357–359 and unity359/362–363/367 distinguish radical national ambition, moderate territorial reform and narrow social bases; Bonaparte policy356–361 makes instrumental French patronage and its limits retrievable.

Named Piedmont/Langhe366–367, Tuscany366–367, Jews367 and Jacobin divisions retrieve the actual comparison: inconsistent popular loyalties, Jacobin local involvement and anti-Jewish attacks complicate a uniform royalist reading. The Piedmont parent lacks supporting365 coercive-alliance treatment, but that is not required to answer this specific367 comparison.
Cispadane359–361, Cisalpine361–363 and Bonaparte/Patriot routes explicitly connect local organization and strategic bargaining to amalgamation, nominated power and continued dependence.

Parthenopean Republic364–365 and Sanfedist/Ruffo routes distinguish withdrawal and reconquest from subsequent royal-court punishment supported by Britain. Ruffo reluctance is not lost by calling all reprisals his programme.

Separate Cispadane, Cisalpine, Ligurian and Roman entries359–363 retrieve different drafting, electoral and command arrangements; local authorship in Liguria is distinguished from French-imposed constitutional and military control elsewhere.

Leoben214–215/217, Venice214–215/217/360–361 and Campo Formio217/361 let the reader follow bargaining and partition as a limit on liberation. Austrian disposal is accessible through the explicit treaty routes, not inferred from unrelated Italian locators.

United Irishmen341–342, rebellion341–343 and Wexford342 retrieve organization, disrupted leadership, divergent elite/peasant expectations and failed French intervention. The broader Irish subject misses a separate368 comparison, but this onset-and-failure demand is fully retrievable in341–343.

Comparative resistance and foreign-support routes350/356/366–368 retrieve declining friends, heterogeneous local conflicts and military overstretch, followed by the Italian collapse368. No universal nationalist unity is implied.

Rhineland incorporation351–352, extraction352–353 and resistance353 can be compared with Belgian Peasants War349–350. The passages separate passive local resistance from armed insurrection despite related material and religious grievances.

Swiss initiative and strategic context354–355 plus Helvetic occupation355–356 retrieve reformist participation, imposed centralization, Alpine access and financial seizure. Local democratic and religious opposition is not treated as absence of every Swiss initiative.

Coalition and Neapolitan routes339/363–364 expose the failed attack on Rome, Championnet advance and republic formed against Directorial wishes, preserving the diplomatic damage and distinct local sequence.

Roman Republic338/362–363 retrieves imposed constitutional government, military supremacy and religious/fiscal conflict. Fresh direct inspection of source PDF page338 confirms the same Roman Republic passage explicitly narrates Pius VI imprisonment, eighteen months of captivity and death at Valence in August1799. This task therefore succeeds through the named Roman route despite the separate lack of captivity/death locators under the Pius VI personal heading; no unsupported385 page match is needed.
